title: Striped Bass Are in Trouble, and East Coast Anglers Are Worried
summary:
For Bill Jakob, striped bass fishing has been a passion for more than 60 years. He remembers nights off Montauk, New York, casting into crashing waves and catching eight or nine fish, some up to 40 pounds. Many East Coast anglers share his worry: the fish are not showing up like they used to, and young stripers are harder to find.

Scientists say that worry is well founded. Regulators said last week that the fish have had eight years of poor reproduction in the Chesapeake Bay, their key habitat, and the population has declined along the Atlantic coast. Heavy fishing is only part of the story. Warming waters, poor river flow, drought, pollution, and possibly more seals and sharks may also make recovery harder.

Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and spend their early years in estuaries, where rivers meet the sea. Up to 90 percent spawn and grow in the Chesapeake Bay, and they do best in cool, wet springs. When flows are low or temperatures climb too high, fewer young fish join the population, a pattern going back to 2019.

Stripers are prized because they fight hard and can be caught from shore, from Maine to Florida. Industry members say guides, trips, gear, and hotel rooms add up to about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the United States. Losing a top predator that helps balance smaller fish would put that at risk.

Regulators have changed how the fish are measured against size rules, but they have not reduced recreational catch levels. Some fishermen say stricter action, possibly even a temporary pause like one used in the 1980s, may be needed so future generations can catch striped bass. Experts and anglers agree the fish are not replacing themselves fast enough.
why_it_matters: Losing a top predator that helps balance smaller fish could harm coastal ecosystems and put about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs at risk.

background_read: Striped bass are a popular fish that live along the Atlantic coast and are prized by anglers because they fight hard and can be caught from shore.
They hatch in fresh or brackish water and spend their early years in estuaries, where rivers meet the sea, with the Chesapeake Bay as their key habitat.
They do best in cool, wet springs, but when river flows are low or temperatures climb too high, fewer young fish survive to join the population.
As a top predator, striped bass help balance smaller fish in the coastal ecosystem, which is one reason their decline worries both anglers and scientists.
